strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing a genuine gap: extends human-AI collaboration from discrete (Overcooked-AI) to continuous, physics-based environments
Comprehensive benchmark design with 12 diverse maps across three collaboration modes (coordination, awareness, action consistency) and two complementary evaluation tasks
Solid experimental methodology: multiple baselines, AI-AI and human-AI evaluation, ablation studies, user study with 32 participants, and honest limitations discussion
Useful community resource: 1,000+ human-human demonstrations, 720 expert demonstrations with randomized properties, promised code release, and detailed reproducibility information
Consistent empirical improvements validated across metrics and demonstrated with human participants (statistically significant improvement in helpfulness, p=0.017)
Strong experimental practices including failure case analysis and comparison with oracle simulator as upper bound
weaknesses: Critical unresolved technical issue: sub-trajectory recombination validity is acknowledged but not addressed. No analysis of how many generated trajectories violate physical constraints, undermining a core contribution of BASS

Concerning dynamics model performance: 48.7% prediction accuracy on Task 2 (vs 62.5% on Task 1) raises questions about whether the model adequately captures physical constraints when generalizing to unseen attributes

BASS methodology is somewhat incremental: behavior augmentation via pose perturbation is straightforward, dynamics-based action selection builds on acknowledged prior work, and partner action prediction simply reuses the learned policy by state swapping

Weak RL baseline: MAPPO struggles due to continuous space complexity, leaving no competitive RL baseline and making it difficult to assess whether improvements are due to BASS or simply the advantage of behavior cloning with rich data

Limited generalization analysis: no cross-task evaluation (Task 1→Task 2 transfer), evaluation still restricted to 12 maps with only varied object properties, and 'unseen' attributes limited to shape/size/mass variations
Action selection uses only Normalized Final Distance as reward, ignoring other important metrics (waiting time, action consistency) that could enable more sophisticated multi-objective selection
Sub-trajectory matching relies on heuristic discretization (48×48 grid) without justification, and the method's sensitivity to this hyperparameter is unexplored

Limited human validation: only 12 participants actually played against models; 32 total participants with modest per-participant trials; no analysis of whether rated behaviors correspond to actual human-like play
Incomplete statistical analysis: significance testing reported only for helpfulness metric; other results lack formal significance tests despite showing modest differences

strengths: Addresses important problem of physically-grounded human-AI collaboration in continuous environments with physics constraints, filling a gap between discrete environments like Overcooked-AI and real-world tasks

Comprehensive benchmark with 12 carefully designed maps covering three collaboration modes (coordination, awareness, action consistency) and well-motivated physical variations (shape, size, mass, friction)
Substantial dataset collection: 1,000+ human-human demonstrations from 36 participants for Task 1 and 720 for Task 2, providing community value for future research
Thorough experimental evaluation including AI-AI comparisons, human subject studies with 32 participants, ablations, and honest discussion of failure cases and limitations
Consistent empirical improvements: BASS outperforms strong baselines (Diffusion Policy, GRU, MLP, MAPPO) across multiple metrics in both AI-AI and human-AI settings
Detailed reproducibility artifacts: extensive appendices covering hyperparameters, reward settings, human study procedures, and implementation details
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: BASS combines straightforward existing techniques (Gaussian perturbation, trajectory recombination, standard autoencoder+MLP dynamics, greedy action selection) without significant innovation; similar approaches cited in prior work (Wang et al., Yuan et al., Ding et al.)

Critical methodological flaw in behavior augmentation: paper states trajectories are 'valid without explicit validation' and 'we will show in experiments that this works anyway'—this is unsound; no ablation comparing validated vs. unvalidated augmentations or analysis of constraint violations
Small expert sample for Task 2: only 4 expert players generating 720 demonstrations raises overfitting concerns; no validation set reported; sample size not justified

Incomplete generalization testing: (1) Task 1 uses only fixed 12 maps for testing, unclear if train/test splits are properly separated; (2) Task 2 changes object properties but not map layouts; (3) NO evaluation on completely new maps never seen during training—a critical omission

MAPPO comparison fairness concern: extensive dense reward engineering required; sparse rewards fail entirely (Appendix C.3); environment may be poorly suited for RL or reward-sensitive; no ablation of reward design or comparison of alternative RL algorithms

Modest empirical improvements with inconsistent ablations: DP+Augmentation alone achieves TCR=0.47 vs. full BASS TCR=0.50 (only 3% gain from simulation); some baselines show worse performance when only augmentation added (MLP TCR drops from 0.356 to 0.295)

Human study limitations: discrepancy between abstract (32 participants) and appendix (12 volunteers); only comparing BASS vs. DP baseline; minimal statistical testing (one reported p-value without multiple comparison correction); no analysis of objective vs. subjective metric correlations
Partner action predictor oversimplified: simply swaps agent state in agent's policy, creating systematic bias; no comparison with alternative approaches or ablation study on this design choice
Incomplete benchmark design justification: no explanation for why 12 maps, how they were selected, or what physical interactions are excluded; unclear coverage of important physical phenomena

Reproducibility gaps: project page URL missing (unfulfilled), no code availability, dataset access unclear, some hyperparameter choices appear arbitrary (σ=0.002, 48×48 grid discretization) without sensitivity analysis
Limited real-world applicability: 2D physics simulation is highly simplified; no sim-to-real transfer discussion; friction, compliance, and other real physical constraints are idealized

Incomplete analysis of learned models: limited ablation studies (only Table 1), no per-map performance breakdown showing which collaboration types benefit from BASS, no analysis of prediction error characteristics across different scenarios

strengths: Addresses important gap in continuous physical human-AI collaboration, previously understudied compared to discrete environments like Overcooked-AI

Well-designed benchmark with thoughtful maps covering coordination, awareness, and action consistency across three collaboration modes; includes realistic physical constraints and diverse object properties
Substantial human data collection (1,000+ demonstrations from 36 participants for Task 1; 720 from 4 experts for Task 2) with proper IRB approval and participant compensation
Comprehensive experimental evaluation combining AI-AI collaboration, human-AI collaboration, human subject studies (statistically significant at p=0.017), ablations, and failure case analysis
Clear problem formulation as Dec-MDP with appropriate discussion of challenges; solid technical execution with extensive implementation details supporting reproducibility
Practical insights: quantified failure case reductions from {0.797, 0.688, 0.906} to {0.343, 0.563, 0.484}, demonstrating concrete improvements in handoff, assistance detection, and grasping
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: BASS combines known techniques (behavior augmentation via perturbation, standard dynamics modeling with autoencoders+MLP, basic action selection) without significant innovation or deep component analysis

Dynamics model shows substantial prediction errors (37.5% on Task 1, 51.3% on Task 2 vs. oracle simulator in Table 3) with inadequate investigation of failure modes or impact on action selection; unclear how much BASS improvement derives from dynamics vs. action selection mechanism

Behavior augmentation validity concerns: paper claims improvements occur 'without explicit validation' of generated trajectories; small noise std (0.002) and arbitrary discretization (48×48 grid) lack justification; no rigorous analysis of whether invalid trajectories are created

Severe generalization limitations: evaluation restricted to 12 fixed map layouts with zero evidence of transfer to new map structures; Task 2 only tests unseen object properties on known maps; claims about generalization are overstated

MAPPO baseline compromised: Appendix C.3 explicitly states sparse rewards are insufficient, forcing hand-crafted dense rewards (Table 5); this creates unfair comparison with BC methods using raw imitation; better RL reward design might substantially close the gap

Human study discrepancy: main text claims '32 participants' but Appendix I.1 states '12 volunteers'—this inconsistency is concerning; 12 participants is modest statistical power; insufficient detail on how comparisons are structured across rounds
Dataset limitations: Task 1 has ~83 demonstrations per map (sparse); Task 2 uses only 4 expert players (minimal diversity); both far below modern standards for learning-based approaches

Unclear participant count and missing reproducibility details: no mention of code release, dataset release plan unclear, project page URL not provided despite being 'available', and insufficient detail to fully reproduce results

strengths: Addresses genuine gap in human-AI collaboration research: most prior work (Overcooked-AI, Hanabi) uses discrete symbolic spaces, while this work tackles continuous control with realistic physics constraints
Well-designed benchmark with thoughtfully organized 12 maps by collaboration mode and two complementary evaluation tasks targeting different generalization challenges
Comprehensive human dataset (>1,000 demonstrations from 36 participants for Task 1) with quantitative diversity validation showing superior coverage vs. expert/RL baselines
Rigorous experimental evaluation combining AI-AI and human-AI testing with multiple baselines (MLP, GRU, DP, MAPPO) and appropriate metrics (TCR, NFD, WT, AC) with ablations
Sophisticated evaluation protocols addressing reproducibility concerns (cross-group evaluation for Task 1, compositional generalization for Task 2)
Extensive implementation details in appendices support reproducibility; inference speed analyzed for real-time feasibility
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: BASS combines standard techniques (Gaussian noise augmentation, trajectory recombination, latent dynamics models, action selection) without significant algorithmic innovation; multi-agent augmentation extension is incremental

Large performance gap between AI-AI evaluation (Table 2, main results) and human-AI play (cross-group DP: 0.3233→0.3855, DP/BASS: 0.3503→0.6512) raises concerns about whether cross-group protocol truly captures human behavior diversity and ecological validity
Failure rates remain substantial after BASS improvement: {0.797, 0.688, 0.906} to {0.343, 0.563, 0.484}; paper acknowledges limitations remain 'a substantial challenge'
Severely limited scope: single 2D physics domain with only 12 maps; only tested on one additional environment (Overcooked-AI, +15% improvement) with no 3D or robotics validation

Dynamics model and partner prediction underspecified: extremely simple 2-layer MLP architecture (128 units, 32-dim latent) with no ablation on choices; partner action prediction only ~71% accurate but impact on performance unclear

MAPPO baseline appears disadvantaged compared to BC methods despite being standard MARL algorithm; poor RL performance (often worse than MLP) suggests either mismatched task design or unfair comparison, weakening baseline strength

Significant AI-AI to human-AI gap (69% TCR improvement for DP/BASS) undermines whether cross-group evaluation (Table 2 primary results) is valid proxy for human adaptation; Task 2 entirely lacks human evaluation
Dataset quality concerns: Task 1 has highly variable participant contribution (3-5 to 72 demos); Task 2 uses only 4 expert players limiting diversity; no inter-annotator reliability study
Statistical rigor issues: no significance testing for main results despite marginal improvements on some metrics (AC: 0.8337 vs 0.8163, <1% difference)
Key design choices relegated to appendices rather than main text (e.g., 4 action candidates justified in Appendix K); project page URL mentioned in abstract but not provided

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing a genuine gap between discrete collaboration environments and physically-grounded interaction
Comprehensive benchmark design with 12 carefully-designed maps covering three collaboration modes and human demonstration dataset (1000+ pairs Task 1, 700 pairs Task 2)
Multiple evaluation metrics (TCR, NFD, WT, AC) appropriately tailored to physical collaboration beyond simple task completion
Thorough empirical evaluation with multiple baselines, ablations, failure case analysis, and diversity metrics validating dataset quality
Thoughtful evaluation protocols addressing reproducibility (cross-group evaluation for Task 1)
Human subject study with 32 participants provides evidence beyond simulation metrics
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: behavior augmentation via noise and trajectory recombination are straightforward extensions of existing techniques; dynamics model is standard autoencoder+MLP; action selection is conventional sampling and greedy selection

Modest improvements often without statistical significance testing: Task 1 seen 8.3% improvement (0.3233→0.3503) with overlapping error bars; Task 2 improvements ~10-15%; no formal significance tests reported
Partner action prediction accuracy only 71.45% (10% tolerance) substantially limits performance per Table 10, yet no principled solution offered or deep analysis provided
Limited human evaluation: only 12 participants in human study, only comparing DP vs DP/BASS (not all methods); Task 1 uses AI-AI proxy rather than actual human collaboration

Asymmetric and possibly unfair evaluation: MAPPO dramatically underperforms and requires dense task-specific rewards (Appendix F.2); suggests either benchmark mismatch or unfair RL setup; no adequate diagnosis

Benchmark limitations reduce generalizability: 2D physics only (real world involves 3D, deformable objects); joystick control differs fundamentally from robot/human manipulation; 12 structured maps are relatively scripted; Overcooked generalization test (Appendix K) is insufficient
Key design choices lack justification: why 4 action samples? why 32-dimensional latent space? why this autoencoder architecture? sensitivity analyses missing
Augmentation validity claims unsubstantiated: 99% success rate cited but no ablation showing impact of invalid trajectories; noise level σ²=0.002 seems arbitrary with no sensitivity analysis

Statistically rigor issues: standard errors provided inconsistently; no formal significance testing across method comparisons; cross-group evaluation (Task 1) doesn't test generalization to truly new maps

Missing technical depth: overclaimed novelty (e.g., 'first benchmark for continuous low-level control'); limited engagement with motion planning and related literature; incomplete failure mode analysis showing why BASS specifically addresses failures

strengths: Addresses genuine gap in physically-grounded continuous human-AI collaboration benchmarks with clear motivation and solid problem formulation
Comprehensive experimental design with thoughtful evaluation protocols (cross-group validation for reproducibility, multiple metrics capturing collaboration quality)
Excellent reproducibility: IRB-approved human studies, extensive implementation details, dataset diversity quantified, 1,700+ human demonstrations
Significant empirical improvements validated through human studies (0.6512 vs 0.3855 TCR, p=0.017 on helpfulness) with 32 real participants
Technically sound method with clever sub-trajectory recombination for multi-agent behavior augmentation (99% physical validity achieved)
Useful benchmark contribution: 12 carefully designed maps spanning 3 collaboration modes, structural format enabling future extensions
Thorough ablations and analyses demonstrating synergy between augmentation and simulation components
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: BASS combines existing techniques (noise perturbation, trajectory stitching, autoencoders, diffusion policies) rather than introducing fundamentally new ideas
Task 2 data collection bottleneck: only 4 expert players for 720 demonstrations, resulting in lower diversity than crowd-sourced data (Table 1); limits confidence in generalization claims
2D simulation environment creates unclear transfer to real 3D robotic systems; while acknowledged as future work, this limits practical impact and real-world applicability
Behavior augmentation validity concerns: while 99% success rate via boundary matching is good, this is a necessary but potentially insufficient check for physics plausibility of swapped trajectories
Human study scale is acceptable but modest (32 participants); each participant limited exposure per model; larger studies would strengthen claims
Sub-trajectory recombination mechanism insufficiently explained: connection between augmentation and simulation-based selection not made explicit; why do these specifically help together?
Benchmark scope moderate: 12 maps and 2 tasks provide starting point but limited for long-term research; physical variation constrained to 2D shapes/sizes with simple physics
Partner action prediction accuracy not negligible (71.45% at 10% tolerance); over 300-step episodes, errors compound; Table 4 shows gap to oracle simulator remains
